summary: Multiple vulnerabilities have been discovered in Juniper Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor, the most severe of which could allow for arbitrary command execution as root. Session Smart Router is Juniper’s software-based SD-WAN router, and Session Smart Conductor is the management and orchestration platform for a fleet of these routers. Successful exploitation of the most severe of these vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-103406) could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected Conductor. An attacker with root access could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full administrative rights. Because the Conductor manages the router fleet, a compromise could also put every managed site at risk.

summary: XO（Xen Orchestra）は、XCP-ng（またはXenServer）インフラストラクチャを可視化、管理、バックアップ、および委任するためのソリューションです。バージョン6.9.2および6.10.1以前では、RESTクッキーの解析が authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D を {} に変換します。REST認証は、そのオブジェクトを文字列として必要とせずにXOトークンプロバイダーに渡します。トークンコレクションは {} をフィルタリングされていない検索として扱い、その最初のトークンを返します。プロバイダーはそのトークンの所有者として認証し、有効期限切れでなければ認証を完了します。認証済みの /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens ルートは再利用可能なログイントークンIDを返します。この脆弱性は実環境で積極的に悪用されています。この脆弱性はバージョン6.9.2および6.10.1で修正されています。

summary: 攻撃者が Kubernetes クラスター内のコンテナのファイルシステムに書き込み可能な場合、/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf に exec クレデンシャルプラグインを設置できます。次に、誰かがコンテナ k8s の write-config または create コマンドでクラスターの kubeconfig をホストに取り込み、その後 kubectl を実行すると、kubectl はそのプラグインを macOS ホストユーザーとして実行します。これにより、信頼されていない Linux コンテナ内からのファイルシステムアクセスがホスト上で任意のコマンド実行に変わってしまいます。この脆弱性は Container バージョン 1.5.0 で修正されています。

summary: Recognized for Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute. We are proud to share that Rapid7 has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems. Our perspective: less stitching, more stopping threats Most security teams don't struggle to find tools. They struggle to make them work together. We believe SOC analysts lose too much of their day moving between consoles and matching alerts to assets by hand, which is time not spent stopping threats. To us, an integrated approach to security operations means detection, investigation and response working from the same data and the same view, so analysts can get from "what fired?" to "what do we do about it?" faster. The importance of exposure management in the SOC Rapid7 Incident Command, part of the Rapid7 Command Platform, brings together SIEM, SOAR, DFIR, attack surface management and threat intelligence. We built it on the idea that exposure management, and the context it brings, belongs inside the SOC, not next to it. In our view, when an alert arrives with what we know about the asset and how exposed it is, analysts can prioritize what matters instead of working from separate vulnerability reports and alert queues. Context to act, not another console to check We believe adopting an integrated SOC shouldn't be all-or-nothing. Incident Command is available in tiers from Essentials to Ultimate, so teams that want extra coverage can add managed services. That helps resource-pressured teams to start with what they need and grow at their own pace, spending less time building and maintaining integrations and more time on investigations. To us, security operations work best when analysts have the context to act, not another console to check. summary: Rapid7’s annual Security Predictions webinar returns on December 10, bringing our experts together to explore what the year ahead could hold for cybersecurity. Before sharing our predictions for 2027, we’re grading last year’s calls: that geopolitical tensions would reshape cyber threats, insider threats would dominate breach root causes, and context would become the new currency of cyber performance. Register here for the 2027 Security Predictions webinar . As security leaders work through their priorities for 2027, those predictions offer a useful starting point. The year reinforced several of the concerns we highlighted, while developments in attacker behavior and AI added new dimensions to the discussion. Looking at how those themes unfolded helps us understand what remains relevant and where our thinking needs to evolve. Geopolitics shaped cyber targeting, with businesses caught in the middle Our prediction that geopolitical fault lines would redraw the cyber battlefield earned an A-, as regional conflicts created opportunities for espionage, disruption, and public pressure throughout 2026. Cyber operations allowed adversaries to pursue those objectives below the threshold of open warfare, with commercial organizations exposed alongside government and critical infrastructure targets. Rapid7 Intelligence tracked a spike in retaliatory activity following regional military escalations in late February. State-directed actors pursued espionage and data theft, while hacktivist personas amplified the impact. Rapid7 also assessed that stolen information was likely to be passed from state actors to hacktivist groups for public release, extending the consequences of an intrusion beyond the initial compromise. That chain from state actor to hacktivist release makes an organization’s exposure harder to judge from its own location or industry alone. Customers, suppliers, infrastructure, and perceived political associations can attract attention, bringing a seemingly routine commercial relationship into a much wider conflict. Examining those dependencies during response exercises uncovers difficult decisions early, particularly where protecting a service or containing an incident requires agreement across security, operations, legal, and executive leadership. Insider risk expanded beyond human users Our prediction that insider threats would dominate breach root causes drew attention to risks ranging from employee negligence to deliberate access selling. During 2026, reporting on ransomware recruitment attempts reinforced concerns about attackers seeking cooperation from people inside organizations, while the growing use of AI agents broadened the conversation about insider risk. As agents gain access to business systems and take actions on an organization’s behalf, questions about permissions, oversight, and unintended consequences increasingly extend beyond human users. Our blog on insider recruitment in ransomware campaigns explored an approach by Medusa to a BBC journalist, offering payment in exchange for access. It illustrated how attackers combine financial incentives, persuasion, and pressure to pursue legitimate credentials, giving organizations a concrete reason to include recruitment attempts in awareness programs and response planning. The wider access economy also remained significant, although credentials appearing for sale do not establish that an employee willingly supplied them. External compromise and exposed systems continued to provide routes into businesses, with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery adding further pressure. Our prediction captured an important concern, while the year reinforced the need to distinguish deliberate insider cooperation from other ways attackers obtain and misuse access. Context proved its value, although we overstated its novelty Our prediction that context would become the new currency of cyber performance earned a B, largely because understanding an environment has always been fundamental to protecting it. During a year shaped by AI-driven vulnerability discovery, however, the ability to connect a new finding with exposed systems, attacker activity, and business consequences became particularly valuable when teams had little time to decide how to respond. Our analysis of the ASOS incident explored that challenge after an unauthorized notification reached customers through the retailer’s own app. With the route of compromise still unclear, the incident raised questions about access to customer communications platforms and how investigators connect activity across accounts, integrations, and third-party services. The same need for context applies to remediation, where an advisory alone cannot determine whether interrupting a critical service is justified. Teams need to know where affected technology is running, how attackers could reach it, and which mitigations are practical. Bringing asset information, threat intelligence, and operational knowledge together remains essential to making those decisions with confidence. Bringing those lessons into our 2027 predictions Across all three themes, the year reinforced how closely security decisions depend on understanding relationships: between organizations, between identities and access, and between technical weaknesses and business consequences. Those connections will remain relevant as AI changes how technology is used and how threats develop. Join Rapid7’s Security Predictions webinar on December 10 to explore those shifts with our experts and consider what they could mean for your priorities in the year ahead. Register for the webinar.

summary: Overview On November 24, 2026, Broadcom released VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0011 to address several new vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123903 , a critical authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned it a CVSSv3.1 score of 9.8 Critical . An attacker who can reach an affected vCenter’s VMware Directory Service (vmdir) over the network can gain access without authenticating. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ distinguishes CVE-2026-123903 from an older vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 , which Rapid7 covered previously when CVE-2026-123890 was reported as being exploited in the wild. Both of these vulnerabilities affect the VMware Directory Service in vCenter and can give an attacker access to the vCenter without credentials. CVE-2026-123890 was reachable over RPC while CVE-2026-123903 is reachable over LDAP. As of this writing, there are no known public reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-123903 in the wild. A public proof-of-concept exploit is available and has been validated by Rapid7 to successfully achieve an authentication bypass. Attackers are known to be targeting vulnerabilities in the VMware Directory Service, therefore Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an urgent basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor updates are available for CVE-2026-123903. Broadcom lists no workaround , and these vCenter updates are not eligible for Quick Patch. Rapid7 recommends updating affected deployments on an urgent basis, outside normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for the deployment. Broadcom lists the following available fixed versions to remediating CVE-2026-123903. These fixed versions also remediate several other high and medium severity CVEs from the same advisory (CVE-2026-123904, CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, CVE-2026-123907, CVE-2026-123908, CVE-2026-123909): VMware Product Affected Version Fixed Version / Patch VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x 9.1.2 VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x 9.0.2.0300 VMware vCenter 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 Contact Broadcom Support (extended-support customers) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform 3.0 , 4.x , 5.0.x , 5.1.x , 5.2 KB463501 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 KB463501 Note that if vCenter 8.0 U3m was previously installed when remediating CVE-2026-123890, it also fixes CVE-2026-123903 and no further vCenter update is needed. For the latest affected-version and remediation guidance, refer to Broadcom's security advisory and supplemental FAQ . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management (InsightVM), and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-123903 on VMware vCenter Server with an unauthenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the November 25, 2026 content release. Intelligence Hub Customers leveraging Rapid7’s Intelligence Hub can access Suricata detection rules for detection of the public CVE-2026-123903 exploit. Updates November 25, 2026: Initial publication. November 25, 2026: Add Intelligence Hub section.

summary: CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: rcloneのバージョン1.67.0から1.76.0未満には、Uloztoバックエンドに資格情報漏洩の脆弱性があります。この脆弱性は、ダウンロード時に認証されたf.restクライアントが使用され、f.cdnではないため、HTTPリダイレクト時にX-Auth-TokenおよびX-User-Tokenヘッダーが意図しないホストに送信されてしまうことに起因します。攻撃者はCDNのダウンロードトラフィックを観察またはリダイレクトできる場合、長期間有効なAPIキーおよびセッショントークンを取得し、被害者のUloztoストレージに対して永続的にアクセスできる可能性があります。

summary: SSSDに脆弱性が発見されました。LDAP（Lightweight Directory Access Protocol）のシャドウ属性を使用してアカウントの有効期限を強制するように設定した場合、SSSDは有効期限の値がゼロであるアカウントを期限切れとして認識しません。有効期限が切れたアカウントの有効な認証情報を持つユーザーは、この脆弱性を悪用してアクセス制御を回避し、システムへの認証を行うことが可能です。これにより、アカウントが無効化されるべき時点を過ぎても不正なアクセスが継続する恐れがあります。

summary: OpenEMR 8.4.0以前のバージョンには、患者ポータルのOnsiteDocumentクエリAPIにマスアサインメントの脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性により、リクエストパラメータでビット単位の条件フィルターが設定され、その値がSQLのWHERE句に引用符なしで挿入されます。認証済みの患者ポータルユーザーは、Id_BitwiseAndなどのパラメータを介してSQLインジェクションを実行し、他の患者の記録やスタッフのパスワードハッシュを含む任意のデータベーステーブルを読み取ることが可能です。

summary: OpenEMRのバージョン7.0.1から8.4.0より前のバージョンには、src/Common/Auth/OneTimeAuth.phpに脆弱性が存在します。このファイルはenforce_onetime_useおよびmax_access_countフラグを無視し、消費されたservice_authトークンを一度も取り消しません。また、rate limitingや厳密な比較なしにlogin_pinをチェックします。攻撃者がキャプチャしたトークンを保持している場合、それをリプレイしたり、PINをブルートフォース攻撃で突破したりして、患者ポータルのセッションを開き、PHI（個人健康情報）を露呈させることが可能です。

summary: OpenEMR 8.3.0より前のバージョンには、FaxSMSモジュールのRCFaxClientおよびSignalWireClientのdisposeDocument関数にパストラバーサルの脆弱性が存在します。これにより、認証された権限の低いユーザーが、未検証のfile_pathパラメータを通じて任意のファイルの読み取りおよび上書きを行うことが可能となります。攻撃者はaction=downloadをリクエストすることで、sqlconf.phpのデータベース資格情報や鍵などの平文ファイルを取得でき、またaction=setupを使用してウェブサーバー上の書き込み可能なファイルを暗号文で上書きすることが可能です。

summary: AIOHTTPは、asyncioとPython向けの非同期HTTPクライアント／サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4以前では、WebSocketのハンドシェイクなどアップグレード対象としてマークされたリクエストが処理されている間、aiohttpは追加で受信したすべての接続データをサイズ制限やフロー制御なしにバッファリングします。これにより、リモートの攻撃者がアップグレード要求の背後でデータをストリーミングし、アップグレードを即座に受け入れもしなければ拒否もしないハンドラーに対して、無制限のメモリ消費を引き起こす可能性があります。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されています。

summary: Overview An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012. The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. The context handles use predictable UUIDv1 values. By creating two reference contexts around a pending login, an attacker can narrow the hidden login handle to a short timestamp window and ask the server for its key. We reproduced the bypass against vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400, build 23929136 , running Photon OS 4.0, and leveraged the resulting administrator connection through to root command execution. SSH and Bash access were initially disabled. The attack recovered the directory database and its Security Token Service (STS) signing key, forged an administrator API session, and used appliance administration features to create an account and enable SSH. Neither the existing SSO password nor the root password was an input to that chain. Impact The attacker needs network access to TCP 2012 and the name of an existing SSO principal. Our PoC uses the default SSO administrator principal, administrator@vsphere.local ; deployments using a different SSO domain need the corresponding account name. The attack does not depend on an existing authenticated connection or an administrator being online. The attacker initiates the login attempt in order to recover its session key. The authenticated connection can call the directory database-copy interface. Its raw database contains the STS private signing key, allowing the attacker to sign administrator assertions that vCenter trusts. Our attack workflow used a forged assertion to create a local appliance superAdmin account, enable SSH and Bash, and execute commands as root through sudo. This final part requires access to the HTTPS API on TCP 443 and SSH on TCP 22, in addition to TCP 2012. It uses the administrative privileges obtained through the original bypass; no second vulnerability is needed once you have administrative RPC access. Technical Analysis Returning the key before checking the proof // vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcsrpserv.c long Srv_rpc_srp_verifier_get_session_key( handle_t hServer, srp_verifier_handle_t hSrp, rpc_p_srp_bytes_container ret_key_cont) { // ... struct SRPVerifier ver = (struct SRPVerifier *) hSrp; //[A1] rpc_p_srp_bytes_container key_cont = NULL; if (!ver) { sts = rpc_s_invalid_handle; goto error; } key = srp_verifier_get_session_key(ver, &key_len); // [A2] if (!key || key_len == 0) { sts = rpc_s_auth_nokey; goto error; } sts = _srp_bytes_container_allocate(key, key_len, &key_cont); if (sts) { goto error; } *ret_key_cont = key_cont; // [A3] // ... } The SRP RPC getter receives an SRP verifier at [A1], obtains its session key at [A2], and returns a copy at [A3]. It checks whether the verifier and key exist. It does not check whether the caller has authenticated, whether the caller owns the verifier, or whether the SRP client has supplied a valid password proof. The value at [A1] is a server-side pointer that the RPC runtime resolves from the context handle supplied in the request. Each newly created verifier context receives its own UUID, so the attacker needs the handle for the specific pending login they want to complete. These context UUIDs identify individual verifier instances; the fixed interface UUIDs identify the available RPC interfaces. UUIDv1 values contain a timestamp, clock sequence, and node identifier. The attacker creates a verifier immediately before starting the target login and another immediately afterward, obtaining both reference UUIDs without authenticating. On the tested service, the reference UUIDs share their clock sequence and node identifier. The attacker reuses those fields and searches the intervening timestamps for the pending login's live verifier, keeping the login connection open throughout the search. // vmdir/thirdparty/csrp/srp.c int srp_verifier_is_authenticated(struct SRPVerifier *ver) { return ver->authenticated; // [A4] } // ... const unsigned char *srp_verifier_get_session_key( struct SRPVerifier *ver, int *key_length) { if (key_length) *key_length = hash_length(ver->hash_alg); return ver->session_key; // [A5] } The underlying SRP library exposes the authentication flag separately at [A4]. Its key getter at [A5] does not consult that flag. The server has already computed the shared key while generating its challenge, because it needs that key to verify the client's proof. Returning it at this stage gives the client the secret needed to produce that proof. Resolving another connection's context // dcerpc/idl_lib/ctxeectx.c void rpc_ss_ee_ctx_from_wire( ndr_context_handle *p_wire_context, rpc_ss_context_t *p_context, volatile error_status_t *p_st) { // ... p_uuid = &p_wire_context->context_handle_uuid; // [B1] // ... nil-handle check and table lock ... this_link = &context_table[dce_uuid_hash(p_uuid, (error_status_t *)p_st) % CALLEE_CONTEXT_TABLE_SIZE]; // [B2] while (!dce_uuid_equal(p_uuid, &this_link->uuid, (error_status_t *)p_st)) { this_link = this_link->next_context; // ... reject a missing entry ... } *p_context = this_link->user_context; /* [B3] */ // ... } The RPC runtime takes the supplied UUID at [B1], searches a process-wide table at [B2], and returns the associated context at [B3]. There is no comparison with the requesting connection or its authenticated identity. Although context creation records a client for lifetime management, that client is not part of this lookup's authorization decision (hooray!!). We confirmed the boundary directly: one anonymous RPC connection created an SRP verifier, and a second anonymous connection retrieved that verifier's key before any password proof was sent. The first connection's context handle was enough to make the second connection's request succeed. The service registers the helper with a secure-interface flag and an authentication callback. On the tested TCP path, however, the RPC executor retrieves those registration values and dispatches the server stub without enforcing the callback. Other directory handlers perform their own access checks. The SRP key getter has no equivalent check, leaving it reachable before authentication. Predictable handles make the lookup usable // dcerpc/uuid/uuidsys.c void uuid__get_os_time(dce_uuid_time_t *uuid_time) { // ... if (gettimeofday(&tp, (struct timezone *)0)) // [C1] { perror("uuid__get_os_time"); exit(-1); } uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_sec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_SEC, &utc); uuid__uemul((long)tp.tv_usec, UUID_C_100NS_PER_USEC, &usecs); // [C2] UADD_UVLW_2_UVLW(&usecs, &utc, &utc); // ... add the UUID epoch offset ... The UUID timestamp generator reads the wall clock at [C1] and converts its microseconds into 100-nanosecond UUID ticks at [C2]. The resulting UUIDv1 handle also contains a clock sequence and node identifier. In our captures, those latter fields remain stable while newly created contexts advance through the timestamp space. vmdir manages this SRP authentication exchange through the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), which provides a common interface for authentication mechanisms. Starting the login creates an SRP verifier internally, but the login client does not receive its context handle. An attacker can obtain reference handles by creating ordinary SRP verifiers through the helper interface. Creating one immediately before the GSS-API login and another immediately afterward bounds the timestamp of its hidden verifier. The shared node and clock-sequence fields then let the attacker construct candidate UUIDs within that interval. The default search advances in increments of ten UUID ticks, matching the clock's microsecond resolution. The generator also supports uniqueness adjustments within a clock tick, so the PoC includes a one-tick search mode. Clock changes, concurrent activity, and the chosen search bounds can affect recovery; exhausting the window does not establish that a target is patched. Exploit Narrowing the Search Window for a Pending Login The service exposes two relevant RPC interfaces on port 2012: Interface UUID Operations used SRP verifier helper c7e94609-6ab0-4767-8e92-b6485bff1649 Create verifier, retrieve key, delete verifier vmdirdbcp 72c780fe-af6b-42ba-9b02-f61f4ccc98ed SRP-authenticated bind, directory state, and database open/read/close The helper's operation numbers are 0 for verifier creation, 1 for key retrieval, and 4 for deletion. GetState is operation 4 on the separate vmdirdbcp interface. The interface UUID is therefore part of identifying an operation; the operation number alone is ambiguous. The client first creates a reference verifier, starts a separate SRP login as the target principal (e.g. administrator@vsphere.local), and creates the second reference verifier. It keeps the login connection open while querying candidate handles over another anonymous connection. These are all connections controlled by the attacker. GSS does not return the handle for its own verifier. A reference verifier for the same principal has a different session key, so retrieving that reference key does not complete the pending GSS login. We need the key from the verifier associated with the login connection; the reference handles only narrow the search for it. In the final standalone PoC test, the reference handles were: Before: 1d98c67a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35 Hidden: 1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35 After: 1d9a8a14-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35 The interval between the reference timestamps was 115,610 UUID ticks, or about 11.56 milliseconds. The search recovered the hidden handle shown above after 5,083 queries. Four workers issued the queries in that Python test, so the count includes requests that were already in flight when the match was found. The SRP verifier helper returns the pending login's actual 20-byte session key. The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. Completing SRP with the disclosed key M1 = SHA1((SHA1(N) XOR SHA1(g)) || SHA1(I) || s || A || B || K) HAMK = SHA1(A || M1 || K) Here, I is the requested principal, N and g are the SRP group parameters, s is the server's salt, and A and B are the public values exchanged during login. The server sends s alongside B in its initial SRP challenge, before the client supplies a password proof. The salt is public: a legitimate client uses it with the password to derive the values needed for authentication. The client already has all of these inputs except K . Once the key getter supplies K , the client can calculate the normal client proof, M1 , and verify the server's response, HAMK . The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. Our client uses the valid public value A = 2 in the normal 2048-bit group. The reference verifiers use the cheaper 1024-bit group only to obtain the timing bounds. The implementation hashes minimal big-endian integer representations. On the tested build, the returned B is 276 bytes because CSRP serializes k*v + g^b without first reducing the sum modulo N . Reducing or truncating that returned value while building the transcript produces the wrong proof. The successful mechanism on this build is the legacy SRP OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.10 . Its token framing also differs from a conventional GSS wrapper: the outer length covers the OID, with the SRP state token following it. The client carries the exchange in SPNEGO bind and ALTER_CONTEXT messages, using RPC packet privacy. Matching that framing is necessary to reach the vulnerable authentication flow. Proving the authenticated connection The client derives packet-protection keys from the recovered SRP key using the server's normal implementation. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 expands the key into 64 bytes using the principal as salt and 128 iterations. Those bytes supply an IV, material for the Kerberos AES-256 string-to-key operation, and a 16-byte HMAC key. RPC stubs are encrypted with AES-CBC and authenticated with HMAC-SHA1 over the ciphertext. PoC output: {"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.919835+00:00", "event": "session_key_disclosed", "uuid": "1d99c43a-e468-11f1-b101-000c29451b35", "key": "1f1476617a050b8e30388e0f58ed80d83f01aa02", "guesses": 5083, "seconds": 0.8774298130301759} {"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:25.952425+00:00", "event": "srp_authentication_complete", "username": "administrator@vsphere.local", "M1": "af03ad96cb799381bf8e9a30a412b4371e24729d", "HAMK": "537b2d5753f213304824551077bddd51ed6693ae", "password_supplied": false} {"time": "2026-11-19T22:25:26.226964+00:00", "event": "protected_rpc_result", "operation": "RpcVmDirGetState", "state": 3, "status": 0, "plaintext": "0300000000000000"} We used RpcVmDirGetState to test the resulting connection to 192.168.1.81 . An anonymous request returned status 5, ACCESS_DENIED . The authenticated request above returned 0300000000000000 : the little-endian directory state, 3 ( Normal ), followed by the operation's success status, 0. The PoC checked the server's SRP proof and the encrypted response's MAC before accepting the result. Key recovery took approximately 0.88 seconds in this run. The complete test retained the original RPC traffic and a packet capture with 15,343 packets and zero kernel drops. This brings us to the end of exploiting CVE-2026-123890. We have demonstrated how we can authenticate to VMware vCenter's directory service as the administrator user and will now outline how that access can be used to get root access to the device. Reading the directory database vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c , Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile : // vmdir/server/vmdir/rpcserv.c UINT32 Srv_RpcVmDirOpenDatabaseFile( handle_t hBinding, PWSTR pwszDBFileName, vmdir_dbcp_handle_t *ppFileHandle) { // ... DWORD dwRpcFlags = VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_ALLOW_TCPIP | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTH_TCPIP | VMDIR_RPC_FLAG_REQUIRE_AUTHZ; // ... dwError = _VmDirRPCCheckAccess(hBinding, dwRpcFlags, pszDomainDn, &pAccessToken); // [D1] BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError); // ... validate arguments and convert the filename ... dwError = _VmDirRemoteDBCopyWhiteList(pszDBFileName); // [D2] BAIL_ON_VMDIR_ERROR(dwError); // ... if ((pFileHandle = fopen(pszDBFileName, "rb")) == NULL) { // ... report the open failure and take the error path ... } *ppFileHandle = pFileHandle; // [D3] // ... The database-copy handler requires authentication and authorization at [D1]. The earlier bypass satisfies those checks as the SSO administrator. The filename passes a database-path allowlist at [D2], and the handler returns a file context at [D3]. We requested /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb through that interface. The IDL assigns operation 0 to open, 1 to read, and 2 to close. The open request carries a reference wide string and an initially empty context handle. Each read supplies the returned context, a byte count, and an empty output container. Reads continue until the server returns a zero byte count. Our first complete export contained 16.22 MB. We used 2,048-byte reads so the response, encryption padding, and verifier fit into a single RPC fragment. The directory stayed in state 3, Normal ; we did not call RpcVmDirSetBackendState or take the service offline. These calls copy the live file rather than producing a transaction-consistent backup. The downloaded file contained the signing credential needed for the next step. Signing an administrator API assertion The TenantCredential-1 record in data.mdb contains the STS RSA private key and its certificate chain. Metasploit already provides extraction and SAML-signing code in vcenter_offline_mdb_extract and vcenter_forge_saml_token . We reused those implementations, matched the signing certificate to the recovered private key, and verified its VMCA issuer. The signed assertion identifies administrator@vsphere.local and carries the existing template's administrator group claims, including SystemConfiguration.Administrators . The issuer uses the appliance's STS identity, and the assertion includes a short validity window. Once the XML is signed, changing its whitespace can invalidate the digest, so the client preserves its compact serialization. lib/msf/core/exploit/remote/http/vmware_vcenter.rb , API login: token = Base64.strict_encode64(Zlib.gzip(assertion)) # [E1] response = vcenter_api_request( 'POST', %w[com vmware cis session], port: port, host: host, headers: { 'Authorization' => "SIGN token=\"#{token}\"" } ) session_id = vcenter_api_value(response) # [E2] The client gzip-compresses and Base64-encodes the assertion at [E1], following the vendor REST SDK's SAML login example . A successful POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session returns the API session ID at [E2]. Subsequent requests carry it in the vmware-api-session-id header. Our forged assertion returned HTTP 200 and authorized reads of the appliance's SSH and Bash settings. From the appliance API to root The authenticated API session gives us a way to create credentials that SSH will accept. We created a fresh local account through the appliance local-accounts API , assigning the superAdmin role. This is an operating-system account on the appliance; creating it does not require changing an existing account's password. The tested build accepts the account-creation request through the legacy REST route POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/<username> , with its configuration inside a config object. The configuration supplies the generated password, roles: ["superAdmin"] , and enabled: true . The same API session enables SSH with PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh and {"enabled":true} , then enables Bash with PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell and {"config":{"enabled":true,"timeout":600}} . /etc/sudoers.d/applmgmt on the tested appliance: %superAdmin ALL= PASSWD: ALL, NOPASSWD: OPERATOR_N, ADMINISTRATOR_N That sudo rule allows the new account to run commands as root using its own generated password. An SSH login initially enters the appliance CLI, so the client requests a PTY and starts shell /bin/bash . After answering the appliance's sudo password prompt, it starts sudo -n /bin/bash -i on the same terminal. The sudo timestamp from that authentication permits the retained root shell. We verified uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) through the resulting SSH connection. This account and password were created by the forged API session; the supplied lab root credentials were used separately for inspection and were not used to obtain this shell. Using the sessions in Metasploit [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered the pending session key after 17337 guesses in 8.12 seconds [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Recovered context 688f5878-e487-11f1-b101-000c29451b35, key f56a33e23fad8b8d340c8ca0887aebe1fb793bab [+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Authenticated as administrator@vsphere.local without a password; protected directory state: 3 [+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Saved authentication evidence to /Users/jheysel/codex_research/vsphere_armory_castle_20261119/metasploit/config/loot/20261119190933_default_192.168.1.81_vmware.vmdir.srp_059381.json [*] VMware directory RPC session 3 opened (192.168.1.70:61547 -> 192.168.1.81:2012) at 2026-11-19 19:09:34 -0700 [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with vmdir session 3; use background to return to msfconsole vmdir > whoami Authenticated SSO principal: administrator@vsphere.local vmdir > state Directory state: 3 vmdir > state Directory state: 3 The Metasploit module separates the inexpensive key-disclosure check from the full authentication attempt. check creates an owned verifier and asks for its key through a second anonymous association. run then performs the pending-login search, completes SRP, and verifies the protected operation. The module's default RPC action retains the authenticated association and exposes a vmdir > prompt with state and whoami commands. Selecting ACTION SHELL continues through database export, SAML API authentication, and SSH to a root command shell. The fresh end-to-end test produced the following output: [+] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Root execution verified: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) [*] Command shell session 1 opened (192.168.1.70:62059 -> 192.168.1.81:22) at 2026-11-20 07:48:25 -0700 ... [*] 192.168.1.81:2012 - Interacting with shell session 1; use background to return to msfconsole ... root [ /home/sebastian-fritsch ]# id uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),4044(shellaccess) CreateSession defaults to true for either action. We resumed the root shell and ran id to show root access before exiting. The shell action saves the generated account credentials and original SSH/Bash settings before changing the appliance. It retains the temporary account and access settings while the session is open. On exit, it closes SSH, restores the original settings, and deletes its account through the API. The order matters: the appliance refuses to delete an account that still has running processes, and disabling SSH terminates active connections. Closing the console abruptly can prevent cleanup; the saved recovery details identify the account and settings to restore. Detection opportunities The unauthenticated key queries are visible before the client establishes packet privacy. Useful network evidence includes repeated calls to operation 1 on the SRP helper interface, with no RPC authentication verifier and context UUIDs that differ mainly in their timestamp fields. In our reproduction, those queries occur between the pending login's initial bind and its SRP proof continuation. The helper interface UUID, operation number, authentication state, query volume, and UUID pattern are useful together. A connection to port 2012 or an administrator SRP login on its own does not establish exploitation. The appliance also retains evidence of the database export and subsequent administration. We recovered the following records from the same vCenter 8.0.2.00400 appliance after the test accounts had been removed. /var/log/vmware/vmdird/vmdird-syslog.log : 2026-11-20T14:45:46.792144+00:00 info vmdird t@140450245629504: Remote DB transfer (/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) granted. The directory service records this message when its filename allowlist grants a remote database-copy request. It identifies the requested database, but does not include the caller's address or prove that the transfer completed. An unexpected grant for data.mdb provides a timestamp to correlate with network traffic and the later API activity; legitimate directory replication can also use this interface. The SRP bypass can occur without a database-copy request, so this entry identifies the export stage. /var/log/vmware/vapi/endpoint/endpoint-access.log : 2026-11-20T14:48:08.065Z | vAPI-I/O dispatcher-0 | e97ae44e-a503-4b58-9b68-1168c80e89c6 | 192.168.1.70 - - [20/Nov/2026:14:48:07 +0000] "POST /rest/appliance/local-accounts/sebastian-fritsch HTTP/1.1" 200 0 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (iPad; CPU OS 17_7_2 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/17.4.1 Mobile/15E148 Safari/604.1" 233 The API access log records the source address, request path, status, and user-agent. This request creates the account used by the root-shell stage. The same file contains our POST /rest/com/vmware/cis/session , PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh , PUT /rest/appliance/access/shell , and eventual account-deletion requests. An HTTP 200 on a settings request does not reveal which value was applied, so the appliance management log supplies the next part of the sequence. /var/log/vmware/applmgmt/applmgmt.log : 2026-11-20T14:48:07 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL created the local account user sebastian-fritsch 2026-11-20T14:48:09 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.ssh.set(enable=True) 2026-11-20T14:48:10 PM UTC [47843]DEBUG:root:com.vmware.appliance.version1.access.shell.set(config=Structure('ShellConfig', dict(enabled=True, timeout=600))) 2026-11-20T14:49:34 PM UTC [47843]INFO:vmware.appliance.localaccounts.localaccounts_impl:Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL deleted the local account user sebastian-fritsch. These records identify Administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL as the account creator and show SSH and Bash being enabled. The configuration values appear in DEBUG-level records on the tested appliance; the account creation and deletion records are INFO-level. The forged SAML session is treated as an administrator session, so that identity alone does not distinguish it from legitimate administration. /var/log/audit/sshinfo.log.1.gz , decompressed: 2026-11-20T14:48:12.368544+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sshd[592859]: Accepted password for sebastian-fritsch from 192.168.1.70 port 62059 ssh2 2026-11-20T14:48:17.298091+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 sudo: sebastian-fritsch : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/sebastian-fritsch ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash -i 2026-11-20T14:49:34.208901+00:00 node-1w7jr9qrllzwd9vncrrr8zlf9 userdel[593806]: delete user 'sebastian-fritsch' The SSH and sudo records tie the new account to the API client's address and a root Bash shell. They also retain the deletion performed during cleanup. Search sshinfo.log and its rotated copies; these entries had moved into sshinfo.log.1.gz by the time we collected them. Matching records are also available through the system journal. /var/log/audit/audit.log: type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186087.886:3732): argc=6 a0="/usr/sbin/useradd" a1="-m" a2="-G" a3="superAdmin" a4="--" a5="sebastian-fritsch" type=EXECVE msg=audit(1795186097.286:3767): argc=4 a0="sudo" a1="-n" a2="/bin/bash" a3="-i" Linux audit records preserve the command arguments for adding the user to superAdmin and invoking sudo -n /bin/bash -i . These examples come from a rotated audit log. They remain available after the account and its home directory are removed, subject to log retention. For this reproduced path, correlate an unexpected database-transfer grant with creation of a local administrator, SSH/Bash enablement, and an SSH login followed by sudo. The database-copy grant appears at 14:45:46 UTC, account creation at 14:48:07, and the root-shell command at 14:48:17. These are administrative operations that can occur legitimately; their sequence and whether they fit expected activity determine their value as indicators. The account name, source address, user-agent, UUIDs, and session values shown here belong to our lab run and are not fixed attacker identifiers. Mitigation Broadcom identifies vCenter 8.0 U3m as the fixed release for the 8.0 branch in VMSA-2026-0009 and its accompanying FAQ . Other release branches have their own guidance. Apply the vendor's supported update for the deployed product and keep the directory-service management interfaces reachable only by the systems that need them. The failed boundary spans both the SRP helper and the RPC runtime: a pending authentication key is exposed, and a connection can resolve a context that it does not own. Replacing predictable UUIDs alone leaves that ownership problem in place. We did not compare the vendor's fixed binaries, so this analysis does not attribute a particular code change to the patch.
summary_excerpt: Overview An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012. The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. summary: CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

The following versions of AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software are affected: C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80 (CVE-2026-127280) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software 1 Vulnerability Heap-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-127280 C-More EA9 Programming Software V6.80 does not adequately validate data read from a project file before using it in heap memory operations. A crafted file causes a heap buffer overrun during file open, resulting in heap corruption and instability within the application. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to open a malicious project file delivered through common distribution channels such as email, file sharing, or removable media. Read More 1 Affected Product AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Update C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads Mitigation If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment. Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-122 Heap-based Buffer Overflow CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 8.4 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments rgod of TrendAI Zero Day Initiative reported this vulnerability to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. summary: この問題は、HTTP/2 を使用する NGINX Plus または NGINX オープンソースの構成に影響を及ぼします。NGINX が未公開のトラフィックを処理する際、フロー制御ウィンドウが許容される閾値を超える可能性があり、その結果、通常は NGINX ワーカーがセグメンテーションフォルトを伴うヒープバッファオーバーフローを引き起こすことがあります。さらに、攻撃者はアドレス空間配置のランダム化（ASLR）が無効化されているシステム、または ASLR を回避できる場合にコードを実行することが可能です。影響としては、攻撃者がこの脆弱性を悪用して NGINX ワーカープロセスをクラッシュさせたり、メモリを破損させたり、遠隔でコードを実行したりする恐れがあります。コントロールプレーンへの影響はなく、これはデータプレーンの問題に限られます。注意点としては、技術サポート終了（EoTS）に達したソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外となります。

summary: NGINX PlusまたはNGINXオープンソースがクライアント接続にHTTP/2を使用するように構成され、クライアントリクエストをバックエンドにプロキシする場合、特別に細工されたリクエストにより、worker_connectionsの残りが少ない状況でワーカープロセスにuse-after-freeが発生する可能性があります。さらに、攻撃者はASLR（アドレス空間配置のランダム化）が無効になっているシステム、またはASLRをバイパスできる場合にコードを実行することが可能です。影響としては、この脆弱性によりリモートの攻撃者がNGINXシステムに対してサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こすか、コードを実行できる恐れがあります。コントロールプレーンは露出せず、これはデータプレーンの問題に限られます。注として、技術サポート終了（EoTS）に達したソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外となっています。

summary: virtualenvは、分離された仮想Python環境を作成するためのツールです。バージョン21.7.12以前では、download_wheel()が定期的な更新や--downloadオプションのために取得されたpipおよびsetuptoolsのseed wheelを、埋め込まれたwheelのBUNDLE_SHA256検証に相当する権威あるダイジェストとバイト単位で照合することなく受け入れていました。改ざんされたインデックス、古くなったミラー、または傍受されたTLS接続により、要求された配布物、バージョン、ファイル名の下で異なるwheelが差し替えられる可能性があり、その結果、virtualenvは攻撃者が制御するwheelをキャッシュし、以降に作成される環境にseedとして組み込みます。この検証はデフォルトのPyPIパスに適用され、PIP_INDEX_URL、PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL、またはPIP_INDEXで独自のインデックスを設定した場合は、再構築されたwheelが正当に公開されている可能性があるため、意図的にスキップされます。この問題はバージョン21.7.12で修正されました。

summary: virtualenvは、隔離された仮想的なPython環境を作成するためのツールです。バージョン21.7.11以前では、PyEnvCfg.write()がプロンプトの値をそのまま行指向のpyvenv.cfgフォーマットに書き込み、PyEnvCfg._read_values()はstr.splitlines()でファイルを解析し、重複するキーに対しては最後の値を受け入れていました。攻撃者が--prompt、VIRTUALENV_PROMPT、または設定入力に影響を与える場合、認識される行区切りや追加のキー（homeを含む）を挿入可能であり、その結果、利用者は攻撃者が選択したベースインタープリターや破損した環境メタデータを使用してしまう可能性があります。このセキュリティ上の影響は、オペレーターの信頼境界外からのプロンプト入力を必要とし、直接供給されたプロンプトの内容は主にオペレーター自身の環境を破損させるものです。この問題はバージョン21.7.11で修正されています。

summary: NGINX Plus または NGINX Open Source がメールプロキシとして設定されている場合、未確認のトラフィックにより nginx ワーカープロセスで use-after-free が発生する可能性があります。さらに、攻撃者は Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) が無効化されているシステム上、または攻撃者が ASLR をバイパスできる場合にコードを実行することが可能です。影響としては、リモートの未認証攻撃者が nginx ワーカープロセスをクラッシュさせるか、メモリを破損させてサービスを妨害する可能性があります。また、リモートコード実行の可能性もあります。制御プレーンには影響がなく、本問題はデータプレーンにのみ関係しています。なお、技術サポート終了（EoTS）に達したソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外としています。

summary: httpブロック内でTLSv1.3が有効な状態で、listenディレクティブにsslパラメータを使用した場合、攻撃者は特殊に細工されたTLS接続を用いてHTTPリクエストボディの読み取り時にNGINXワーカープロセスで無限ループを引き起こすことができます。その結果、ワーカープロセスは新しい接続の受け入れと既存接続の処理を停止します。なお、技術サポート終了（EoTS）に達したソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外とします。影響としては、この脆弱性によりリモートの未認証攻撃者がNGINXのサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こす可能性があります。コントロールプレーンへの影響はなく、データプレーンの問題に限定されています。

summary: 説明: この問題は、HTTP/3を使用するNGINX PlusおよびNGINX Open Sourceの設定に影響を及ぼします。リモートの未認証攻撃者がNGINXワーカープロセスでuse-after-free状態を引き起こし、リスタートを招く可能性があります。攻撃の成功は攻撃者の制御を超えた条件にも依存します。さらに、攻撃者はASLR（アドレス空間配置のランダム化）が無効化されているシステム、または攻撃者がASLRを回避できる場合にコードを実行することも可能です。影響: この脆弱性により、リモート攻撃者がNGINXシステムに対してサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こすか、場合によってはコード実行をトリガーする可能性があります。コントロールプレーンへの露出はなく、本件はデータプレーンの問題に限られています。注意: テクニカルサポート終了（EoTS）となっているソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外としています。

summary: この問題は、NGINX Plus または NGINX Open Source がプロキシとして設定されており、プロキシ対象のサーバ名に変数が含まれ、かつ Server Side Includes（SSI）またはミラーディレクティブが同じサーバ名を解決するロケーションにサブリクエストを送信する場合に発生します。この条件下で、細工されたHTTPリクエストにより、ワーカープロセスで use-after-free 状態が引き起こされる可能性があります。また、アドレス空間配置のランダム化（ASLR）が無効化されているか、攻撃者がASLRを回避できる場合には、コードの実行も可能になる可能性があります。 影響として、攻撃者はこの脆弱性を悪用し、NGINXワーカープロセスをクラッシュさせたり、メモリを破損させたり、リモートコード実行（RCE）を行ったりすることができます。 注意点として、技術サポート終了（EoTS）となったソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外としています。

summary: 説明 NGINX Plus または NGINX Open Source が ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module モジュールを使用して構成されている場合、認証されていない攻撃者による特別に細工された ClientHello メッセージにより、ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module 変数に偽造値が生成され、バーチャルサーバーの選択に影響を与える可能性があります。さらに、TLS 1.3 サポートなしで SSL/TLS 接続を終了するプロキシサーバーとの間で不整合が発生する場合もあります。影響 この脆弱性により、攻撃者は ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module 変数の値を偽造して NGINX システムのストリームルーティングのセグメンテーションを回避できる可能性があります。その結果、攻撃者は到達不可能であるべき特権的または内部のバックエンドへの接続をルーティングし、機密情報にアクセスすることが可能になります。制御プレーンには影響がなく、本件はデータプレーンの問題に限られます。注：技術サポートが終了（EoTS）したソフトウェアバージョンは評価対象外です。

summary: OpenEMR 8.5.0未満には、interface/billing/sl_eob_invoice.phpに格納型クロスサイトスクリプティングの脆弱性があります。このファイルは、請求コードをHTML属性向けにエスケープしますが、インラインのonkeyupハンドラ内のJavaScript文字列向けにはエスケープしません。診療記録のコーディング権限を持つ臨床医は、diagnosis.phpを通じて細工された請求コードを保存可能であり、これによりバックオフィスのユーザーが支払いを入力した際にスクリプトが実行され、患者情報および財務情報が漏洩したり、そのユーザーとしての操作が行われたりする可能性があります。

summary: OpenEMR 8.5.0より前のバージョンには、library/ESign/Form/Controller.phpのesign_form_submitハンドラに認可欠如の脆弱性が存在します。このハンドラはコール元のパスワードのみを検証しており、患者、診察記録、またはフォームの種類へのアクセス権を確認していません。認証されたコアユーザーは任意のformId、formDir、およびencounterIdの値を指定することで、任意の患者の診療フォームに署名およびロックを行い、不正な承認記録を作成し、通常の編集を妨害することが可能となっています。

summary: OpenEMRのバージョン5.0.2から8.5.0未満には、mfa_registrations.phpおよびmfa_u2f.phpに認証が欠落している脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性により、セッションハイジャッカーがパスワードの再入力なしでMFAファクターを削除したり、U2Fキーを登録したりできます。被害者の認証済みセッションを保持している攻撃者は、すべての二要素認証を削除し、自分のU2Fキーを追加できるため、後のログイン時にはパスワードだけでMFAを回避することが可能です。

summary: AIOHTTPはasyncioおよびPython向けの非同期HTTPクライアント/サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4より前のApplication.add_domain()は、ドメインマスク内のアスタリスクワイルドカードをすべて貪欲な正規表現の断片に変換するため、2つ以上のワイルドカードを含むマスクにマッチせず、長いHostヘッダーを拒否するのに多項式時間がかかる可能性があります。リモートの攻撃者は、そのようなヘッダーを複数回送信することで、マルチワイルドカードドメインマスクで設定されたサーバーのイベントループを停止させることができます。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されました。

summary: AIOHTTPは、asyncioとPython向けの非同期HTTPクライアント／サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4以前では、Set-Cookieの解析において認識されないname=value属性を追加のクッキーとして扱っていました。一方で、CookieJarは保存・送信するクッキーの数を制限しません。悪意のあるサーバーは、aiohttpクライアントに非常に大きなクッキーセットを蓄積させることができ、リダイレクトを通じて繰り返しメモリとCPUを消費させ、同一ドメインへの後続リクエストで過度に大きなCookieヘッダーを構築する可能性がありました。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されました。

summary: AIOHTTPはasyncioとPythonのための非同期HTTPクライアント／サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4以前のRequest.post()は、URLエンコードされたフォームボディ内のフィールド数を制限しておらず、多数の繰り返しキーをMultiDictに挿入するとイベントループ上で二次的な遅延が発生します。リモートの攻撃者は、client_max_size以内のフォームPOSTをRequest.post()を呼び出すハンドラに送信して、イベントループをブロックする可能性があります。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されました。

summary: AIOHTTPはasyncioとPythonのための非同期HTTPクライアント/サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4より前のバージョンでは、Content-Transfer-Encodingがbase64に設定されたマルチパートパートをBodyPartReader.read_chunk()で処理する際に、チャンクの長さが4の倍数になるまで読み続けており、バイト制限を強制しませんでした。短いContent-Lengthや長い空白の連続により、一度の呼び出しでサイズチェックの前に残りのボディがメモリに読み込まれたり、イベントループでのスピンが発生する可能性があります。リモートの攻撃者は、そのようなマルチパートリクエストをマルチパートデータを読み取るハンドラに送信し、client_max_sizeをバイパスすることが可能でした。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されました。

summary: AIOHTTPは、asyncioおよびPython向けの非同期HTTPクライアント/サーバーフレームワークです。バージョン3.14.4より前のバージョンでは、C言語製のWebSocketリーダーが符号付き64ビット算術を使用しており、既にバッファリングされている部分的なメッセージのサイズに宣言されたフレーム長を加算していました。2の63乗付近の長さがオーバーフローを引き起こし、max_msg_sizeのチェックを通過させる可能性があります。リモートピアは、小さな非最終フラグメントの後に過大なメッセージを送信し、無制限のメモリ消費を引き起こすことができます。Python製のWebSocketリーダーは影響を受けません。この問題はバージョン3.14.4で修正されています。

summary: NGINX PlusおよびNGINXオープンソースには、aliasディレクティブを使用し、かつrewriteディレクティブとsetまたはreturnディレクティブで$request_filename変数を参照するロケーションが設定されている場合に脆弱性が存在します。また、同様の影響は$request_filename変数がアクセスログフォーマットディレクティブで使用されている場合にも発生する可能性があります。認証されていない攻撃者は、自分の制御外の条件とともに悪意のあるHTTPリクエストを送信することで、この脆弱性を悪用できます。これにより、NGINXワーカープロセスでヒープバッファオーバーフローが発生し、プロセスの再起動を引き起こす可能性があります。さらに、ASLR（アドレス空間配置のランダム化）が無効化されているシステムや、攻撃者がASLRを回避できる場合には、攻撃者がコードを実行することも可能です。影響としては、この脆弱性によりリモートの攻撃者がNGINXシステムに対してサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こしたり、コードの実行を誘発したりする可能性があります。コントロールプレーンに対する影響はなく、この問題はデータプレーンに限られています。注として、技術サポート終了（EoTS）に達したソフトウェアバージョンは評価されていません。

summary: NGINX PlusおよびNGINX Open Sourceには、ngx_http_core_moduleモジュールに脆弱性があります。非同期ファイルI/O（AIO）が特定の構成で有効になっている場合、「include virtual」コマンドを含むServer Side Includes（SSI）ページを処理すると、NGINXワーカープロセスでUse-After-Free（UAF）が発生する可能性があります。これにより、メモリ破損やワーカープロセスのクラッシュが引き起こされる恐れがあります。さらに、攻撃者はAddress Space Layout Randomization（ASLR）が無効化されているシステム、または攻撃者がASLRをバイパスできる場合にコードの実行を行う可能性があります。影響としては、この脆弱性によりリモートの攻撃者がNGINXシステムに対してサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こしたり、メモリを破損させたり、場合によってはコード実行を誘発したりすることが考えられます。コントロールプレーンには影響がなく、データプレーンの問題に限られます。注意点として、技術サポート終了（EoTS）となったソフトウェアバージョンについては評価を行っていません。

summary: OpenEMR 8.3.0より前のバージョンには、保存型クロスサイトスクリプティングの脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性により、CAMOSアクセス権を持つ認証ユーザーがajax_save.phpを介して悪意のあるCAMOSコンテンツを保存し、HTMLを注入できます。攻撃者は、rx_print.phpのnon-print_htmlブランチを通じてエントリが表示される際にスクリプトペイロードがエンコードされずに実行されるため、そのペイロードを保存することができ、被害者ユーザーとして操作を実行したりデータを読み取ったりできます。

summary: OpenEMR 8.4.0より前のバージョンには認可バイパスの脆弱性が存在し、患者スコープのSMARTトークンで他の患者のアンケート回答を読み取ることが可能です。これは、FhirQuestionnaireResponseServiceがIPatientCompartmentResourceServiceを実装していないことが原因です。攻撃者がpatient/QuestionnaireResponse.rsトークンを所持している場合、uuidによる回答要求やフィルタリングされていないバンドルの一覧取得が可能であり、患者を跨いだ臨床評価の回答を入手できます。

summary: OpenEMR 8.4.0より前のバージョンには、ESignルーター（library/ESign/Router.php）にローカルファイルインクルージョンの脆弱性が存在します。このルーターは未サニタイズのmoduleパラメーターを「＜module＞/Controller.php」のrequire_onceに渡します。また、faxモジュールのfaxProcessUploadsは拡張子のチェックを行わずに、攻撃者が名付けたファイルを予測可能な一時パスに書き込みます。認証済みの攻撃者はController.phpというPHPファイルをアップロードし、traversingモジュールパラメーターを用いてinterface/esign/index.phpをリクエストすることで、そのファイルをインクルードして任意のコードを実行可能です。

summary: OpenEMRのバージョン8.3.0以前には、標準REST APIの患者保険および雇用者検索にSQLインジェクションの脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性は、クエリ文字列パラメータの名前をエスケープせずにSQLのカラム識別子として連結してしまうことが原因です。認証済みクライアントや低権限の患者ポータルOAuth2トークンを持つクライアントは、細工したパラメータ名を/api/patient/{puuid}/insuranceまたは/api/patient/{puuid}/employerに送信することで、患者のPHI（個人医療情報）、ユーザーレコード、およびAPIクライアントのシークレットを抽出することが可能です。

summary: Zimbra Collaboration Suite（ZCS）の zmmailboxdmgr ランチャーにローカル特権昇格の脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性により、Unix の zimbra アカウントが root 権限で任意のコマンドを実行できます。パスワードなしの sudo インターフェースは、十分に制限されていない JVM 引数を受け入れます。攻撃者は Jetty の特権降格を遅延させ、OnOutOfMemoryError コマンドを登録し、起動中にヒープの枯渇を強制することで、JVM がまだ root として動作している間にコマンドを実行させることが可能です。悪用するには、メールボックスサーバー上で zimbra としてローカルコマンドを実行し、悪意のある再起動中に mailboxd を中断する必要があります。ZCS のバージョン 10.1.16 および 10.1.21 が影響を受けます。

summary: Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) の MTA パッケージにおけるローカル権限昇格の脆弱性により、Unix の zimbra アカウントが任意のコマンドを root 権限で実行できるようになります。インストールされている sudo ポリシーは、Postfix 管理コマンドのパスワード不要の root 実行を許可しており、その引数を制限していません。攻撃者は Postfix の設定で zimbra が制御する daemon_directory を選択し、postfix set-permissions を呼び出すことで、Postfix に攻撃者の post-install プログラムを root として実行させることが可能です。Postfix の設定ディレクトリは zimbra によって書き込み可能であるため、postconf の制限だけではこの実行経路を排除できません。悪用するには MTA ノード上で zimbra としてローカルコマンドを実行する必要があります。影響を受けるバージョンは ZCS 10.1.16 および 10.1.21 です。
summary_excerpt: Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) の MTA パッケージにおけるローカル権限昇格の脆弱性により、Unix の zimbra アカウントが任意のコマンドを root 権限で実行できるようになります。インストールされている sudo ポリシーは、Postfix 管理コマンドのパスワード不要の root 実行を許可しており、その引数を制限していません。攻撃者は Postfix の設定で zimbra が制御する daemon_directory を選択し、postfix set-permissions を呼び出すことで、Postfix に攻撃者の post-install プログラムを root として実行させることが可能です。Postfix の設定ディレクトリは zimbra によって書き込み可能であるため、postconf の制限だけではこの実行経路を排除できません。悪用するには MTA ノード上で zimbra としてローカルコマンドを実行する必要があります。影響を受けるバージョンは ZCS 10.1.16 および 10.1.21 です。

summary: Apache Roller バージョン 4.0.0 から 6.1.4 において、信頼されていないデータの逆シリアライズにより、認証されていないリモートの攻撃者が任意のコードを実行できる脆弱性があります。XML-RPC エンドポイントはベンダー独自の拡張タイプを受け入れ、認証前にそれらを逆シリアライズします。この脆弱性は CVE-2026-82384 と同一であり、当該CVEでは Apache Roller 6.1.5 のみが影響を受けるとされていました。本問題は現在も積極的に悪用されています。利用者は XML-RPC 機能を無効化する際に拡張タイプも無効化し、XML-RPC リクエストを拒否する Apache Roller 6.1.6 以降へのアップグレードを推奨します。ただちにアップグレードできないユーザーは、WEB-INF/web.xml 内の "enabledForExtensions" を "false" に設定するか、"/roller-services/xmlrpc" サーブレットのマッピングを削除し、Roller を再起動してください。管理 UI で XML-RPC を無効にするだけでは不十分です。古いバージョンでは、該当設定を確認する前にリクエストを逆シリアライズしてしまうためです。

summary: Executive Summary Healthcare’s cyber threat landscape in 2026 extended across providers, research institutions, medical-technology companies, software ecosystems, and organizations entrusted with patient information. Ransomware remained the sector’s most visible operational threat, but credential abuse, data theft, state-sponsored espionage, destructive activity, and supply-chain compromise created additional paths to disruption and exposure. These threats frequently traveled through identities, applications, remote access services, software dependencies, vendors, and other infrastructure beyond the hospital network. This report examines those interconnected risks alongside PolySwarm telemetry on relevant ransomware families and malicious artifacts. The findings show that healthcare resilience increasingly depends on protecting trusted access, evaluating software before deployment, monitoring external dependencies, and preserving operations when technology fails. SCOPE: This report examines threats to the healthcare vertical reported from January 1 through mid-November 2026.

summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: A vulnerability has been discovered in VMware vCenter, which could allow for authentication bypass. VMware vCenter Server is a centralized management platform used to administer VMware vSphere environments, including ESXi hosts and the virtual machines running on them. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. Depending on the privileges associated with the account, an attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights. Accounts configured to have fewer user rights on the system could be less impacted than those that operate with administrative user rights.

The malware combines Android Accessibility Services abuse, hidden virtual network computing (HVNC), credential harvesting, and wireless Android Debug Bridge (ADB) functionality to enable extensive remote control of compromised devices. summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Overview On November 19, 2026, Broadcom published VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0009 , addressing five vulnerabilities in VMware products. The most severe of these, CVE-2026-123890 , is an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel ( CWE-288 ) in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9.8 . A malicious actor with network access to an affected vCenter deployment may exploit CVE-2026-123890 without credentials to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system as the Administrator user. Mandiant privately reported the issue to Broadcom. Also, Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by Chinese state-linked threat actor ARMORY CASTLE as early as September 2026. CVE-2026-123890 is distinct from the vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-59309 that Broadcom addressed earlier in 2026. The vendor FAQ states that all vCenter systems below the versions fixed by VMSA-2026-0009 require the new update, including systems that already received the earlier fix. Broadcom characterizes the vCenter update as an emergency change requiring prompt action. On November 20, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-123890 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. Mitigation guidance Vendor-provided updates are available for CVE-2026-123890. Broadcom lists no workaround, and the patches cannot be applied using vCenter Quick Patch. Organizations should prioritize upgrading vCenter on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for their deployment. VMware Product Affected Version Fixed Version / Patch VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter Server 7.0 Contact Broadcom Support (extended-support customers) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2 8.0 U3m — KB463116 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 8.0 U3m — KB463116 The fixes are cumulative. The vCenter 8.0 U3m and 9.0.2.0200 updates introduce a “Back-in-Time” restriction that blocks upgrades to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1 ; Broadcom advises customers in an active upgrade to review the vendor FAQ and interoperability matrix. Updating vCenter temporarily makes its management interfaces unavailable, but Broadcom states that running virtual machine and container workloads continue to operate. For the latest affected-version and mitigation guidance, please refer to Broadcom's security advisory and supplemental FAQ . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, InsightVM, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-123890 on VMware vCenter Server with an unauthenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the Nov 20, 2026 content release. Updates November 19, 2026 : Initial publication. November 23, 2026 : Added CISA KEV addition to the Overview section.

summary: When an MDR provider contains a compromised endpoint, your team needs to know whether the weakness that enabled the attack exists elsewhere and who is responsible for addressing it. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in. Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses. How does preemptive MDR differ from traditional MDR? Managed detection and response provides security specialists who monitor, investigate, and respond to threats around the clock. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security. Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. When analysts investigate suspicious activity on a server, knowing that it is internet-facing, supports a critical application, and has a vulnerability under active exploitation helps them assess urgency and determine where to look next. In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address. Within a broader preemptive cybersecurity strategy, MDR connects exposure information with the people investigating and responding to threats. The aim is to reduce opportunities for compromise and intervene before an attack causes harm, while retaining the expertise to contain and recover from incidents. How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR helps teams decide which weaknesses require action first. Exposure context also informs targeted hunting and the investigation of suspicious activity. Consider a hypothetical organization running an internet-facing application affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability. The security team needs to establish whether the vulnerable software is present, what the application supports, and whether attackers are exploiting the weakness. Those findings can guide remediation priorities and targeted hunting for signs of compromise. If suspicious activity appears, analysts investigate it with an understanding of the affected system and the potential route an attacker could take through the environment. Depending on the evidence, the response may involve containing a system, examining related accounts, or expanding the investigation to other assets. The organization’s remediation teams also need clear recommendations about the underlying exposure. What the investigation reveals then feeds back into detection rules, hunting priorities, and response procedures. This gives leaders a way to track an identified risk through investigation, action, and outstanding work, with clearer ownership at each stage. What role does AI play in preemptive MDR? Before analysts can assess a potential threat, they often need to retrieve logs, examine user activity, and connect evidence across several systems. AI can accelerate this work by gathering and correlating information for review. Agentic investigation capabilities can perform elements of that process in parallel, test possible explanations, and organize findings. Their usefulness depends on the available data: missing identity activity or asset information can leave gaps in the account of what happened. Rapid7’s approach keeps human expertise central to validation and response decisions. Analysts assess the evidence alongside the organization’s priorities and the consequences of an action, including whether isolating a system could interrupt a critical service. What to look for in a preemptive MDR provider When evaluating a service described as preemptive, ask the provider to show how exposure information changes its work. A redacted investigation should make clear what analysts knew about the affected asset, how that influenced their reasoning, and which actions followed.If an investigation identified a weakness, was it assigned to an owner and addressed? Did the findings change detection coverage or future priorities? Where AI contributed, the provider should explain its role and the oversight applied. Incident response remains part of the requirement. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response alongside exposure-informed defense and AI-assisted investigation, supporting containment, detailed analysis, and threat eradication. Agree on responsibilities before that support is needed. Establish which actions the provider can take, when customer approval is required, and who owns remediation. Those arrangements determine how findings become action, particularly when taking a system offline carries business consequences. Once the service is operating, review progress through specific cases: exposures addressed before exploitation, threats contained, and weaknesses closed after investigation. Ask to see the evidence behind those outcomes and any work still outstanding, so your team can judge where risk has changed and where further attention is needed.
